evals.description: Load classification: classify sections of a skill body by load type

expected_output.section_1_reason: Verbose preamble with no new information — redundant meta-commentary before substance
expected_output.section_2_reason: Comparative table that builds a schema for distinguishing load types — directly promotes schema formation
expected_output.section_3_reason: Worked example that makes the abstract rule concrete — promotes schema through varied instantiation
expected_output.section_4_reason: Redundancy effect — prose restates what the table already communicated clearly

evals.prompt:
Given the following skill body excerpt, classify each section as intrinsic, extraneous, or germane load:

1. A 200-word preamble explaining that 'this section is important because understanding the concept helps agents write better output and therefore is worth reading carefully before moving on to the next section'

2. A table comparing three load types with columns: Name, Definition, Should Eliminate?, Example

3. A worked example showing a before/after of an audit report, with an explanation of why each change reduces a specific load type

4. A paragraph that restates in prose exactly what the preceding table already communicated
expectations: Classifies section 1 (200-word preamble) as extraneous load
Classifies the comparative table (section 2) as germane load — it promotes schema formation
Classifies the schema-formation section (section 3) as germane load
Provides a load-source reason for each classification (not just the label)
Does NOT classify the comparative table as extraneous (this would conflate explanatory structure with redundancy)

evals.description: Prompt redesign: restructure an overloaded single-block prompt using CLT chunking/segmentation

expected_output.approach: Segment into sequential steps, each with a single output
expected_output.step_1: Step 1: Review the skill body. List any sections with extraneous load. Format: [section_name] — [load_source]
expected_output.step_2: Step 2: Check evals/evals.json. Answer: (a) Does it have ≥2 evals? (b) Does each eval cover a distinct use case?
expected_output.step_3: Step 3: Check frontmatter. List any missing v6 required fields. Include verify_with relations status.
expected_output.step_4: Step 4: Write a Linear comment. Group findings as BLOCKING and ADVISORY. Omit NITPICKs.
expected_output.rationale: Each step has a single output type, allowing the model to complete it before holding the next task. The original prompt required simultaneously tracking 5 distinct outputs.

evals.prompt:
The following prompt has high intrinsic load. Restructure it using CLT segmentation to reduce the simultaneous demands on the model's processing capacity:

'Review the attached skill file and identify any sections that have extraneous load, then check whether the eval file has at least two evals and whether each eval covers a distinct use case, and also verify the frontmatter has all required v6 fields including verify_with relations, and finally write a summary Linear comment that covers all findings grouped by severity, making sure to note which findings are BLOCKING versus ADVISORY, but skip anything that is only a NITPICK.'
expectations: Decomposes the multi-step task into 2-4 sequential prompts, each producing a single named output
Each step has a single deliverable defined (no implicit chained reasoning across steps)
Preserves the intrinsic load of each sub-task while removing the extraneous load of simultaneous demands
Names the segmentation strategy explicitly as CLT segmentation (or equivalent: chunking, progressive disclosure)
Does NOT propose a single mega-prompt with bullet-point sub-instructions (this preserves the high simultaneous load)

evals.description: Working memory budget: identify which dashboard layout violates the ~4-chunk limit

expected_output.reason: 10 independent data points with no grouping exceeds the ~4-chunk working memory limit. Reader must process each metric as a separate chunk with no schema to consolidate them.
expected_output.fix: Group metrics into labeled categories (e.g., 'Revenue: gross, net, refunds'; 'Profitability: gross margin %, net margin %'; 'Operations: order count, AOV, fulfillment cost'; 'Marketing: ad spend'). Each category label becomes one chunk that pre-loads a schema for its children.

evals.prompt: A dashboard widget shows: (1) gross revenue, (2) net revenue, (3) refunds, (4) COGS, (5) gross margin %, (6) net margin %, (7) order count, (8) average order value, (9) fulfillment cost, (10) ad spend — all in a single flat grid with no grouping, uniform visual weight, and no category labels. Does this violate CLT working memory limits? If so, what is the fix?
expectations: Returns verdict VIOLATES CLT (or equivalent: too many chunks, exceeds working memory)
Cites the ~4-chunk working-memory limit (Miller's 4±1) as the underlying constraint
Recommends grouping the 10 metrics into 3-4 semantic chunks (e.g. revenue cluster, margin cluster, ops cluster)
Names the intervention as schema-building or progressive disclosure (germane-load promotion)
Does NOT recommend simply removing metrics — the fix is grouping, not subtraction
